ORIGINAL GUIDE FACT EXTRACTION (C:/Users/mitch/dual-agent-harness/examples/field-guide/artifact/GUIDE.md):
F1: Store four litres per person per day, so twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours.
F2: Half for drinking, half for cooking and basic hygiene.
F3: Use food-grade containers, keep them out of direct sunlight, and replace stored water every six months.
F4: With advance warning of a storm, also fill the bathtub.
F5: Use bathtub water for flushing toilets and washing, never for drinking.
F6: Keep a dedicated shelf of non-perishable food for three days: canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, and shelf-stable milk.
F7: Choose foods needing no cooking, and own a manual can opener, since an electric one is useless.
F8: Eat the refrigerator's perishable food first, then the freezer's, and only then the emergency shelf.
F9: An unopened refrigerator keeps food safe about four hours.
F10: A full freezer holds a safe temperature about forty-eight hours, a half-full one only about twenty-four.
F11: Keep it consolidated and full, even with containers of frozen water.
F12: Keep both doors closed as much as possible and tape a reminder note to each.
F13: Discard any perishable food more than two hours above four degrees Celsius.
F14: Use battery-powered LED lanterns or headlamps as your primary light, and avoid candles entirely, a leading cause of house fires during outages.
F15: Store at least one light per person plus two spare sets of batteries for each.
F16: Keep one headlamp beside each bed and one lantern in the kitchen, placed where they can be found in the dark.
F17: Never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator indoors, in a garage, or near a window; each produces carbon monoxide, which is odourless and can be fatal.
F18: Install at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on each floor where people sleep.
F19: In cold weather, pick one small room on a south-facing side, close its door, and gather everyone; layered clothing and blankets beat any improvised heater.
F20: If the indoor temperature falls below ten degrees Celsius and you cannot stay warm, relocate to a warming centre or a neighbour's home.
F21: Keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio for emergency broadcasts, and learn your local emergency station's frequency before the outage.
F22: Charge every phone and power bank whenever a storm is forecast; a full twenty-thousand-milliamp-hour power bank recharges a typical phone roughly four times.
F23: Put your phone in low-power mode as the outage starts, and agree in advance on one out-of-area contact everyone will text, because texts beat voice calls on congested networks.
F24: Keep a first-aid kit and a seven-day supply of every prescription medication, rotating them to stay in date.
F25: Refrigerated medication such as insulin generally stays usable at room temperature up to twenty-eight days, but confirm the rule for your medication with a pharmacist before an emergency.
F26: Write your pharmacy, doctor, and poison-control numbers on paper, because a dead phone is not a phone book.
F27: Wait five minutes before switching major appliances back on, letting the grid stabilise.
F28: Check the freezer: food still holding ice crystals can be safely refrozen.
F29: Restock everything used within one week, starting with water and batteries.
F30: Finally, write a one-page note on what was missing or awkward, and fix at least one gap before the next outage.
